public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 353

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/353](https://www.erdosproblems.com/353)
- [Er83d] Erdős, Paul, *Some combinatorial, geometric and set theoretic problems in measure
  theory*. Measure Theory, Oberwolfach 1983 (1984), 321-327.
- [Ko23] Kovač, V., *Coloring and density theorems for configurations of a given volume*.
  arXiv:2309.09973 (2023).
- [KoPr24] Kovač, V. and B. Predojević, *Polygons of unit area with vertices in sets of infinite
  planar measure*. arXiv:2412.11725 (2024).
- [Ko25] J. Koizumi, *Isosceles trapezoids of unit area with vertices in sets of infinite planar
  measure*. arXiv:2501.01914 (2025).
-/

@[expose] public section

open Affine EuclideanGeometry MeasureTheory

open scoped Real

namespace Erdos353

/--
Let $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be a measurable set with infinite measure. Must $A$ contain the
vertices of an isosceles trapezoid of area $1$? What about an isosceles triangle, or a
right-angled triangle, or a cyclic quadrilateral, or a convex polygon with congruent sides?

Koizumi [Ko25] has resolved this question, proving that any set with infinite measure must
contain the vertices of an isosceles trapezoid, an isosceles triangle, and a right-angled
triangle, all of area $1$.

This statement formalizes the leading question, for isosceles trapezoids; the remaining
configurations are given as variants below. The area of a polygon is taken to be the Lebesgue
measure of the convex hull of its vertices.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 28 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/110d489ed5c07e5b216453e092e9113127c98c9a/problems/353/Erdos353.lean"]
theorem erdos_353 : answer(True) ↔
    ∀ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A → volume A = ⊤ →
      ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, ∃ c ∈ A, ∃ d ∈ A,
        IsIsoscelesTrapezoid a b c d ∧
        volume (convexHull ℝ {a, b, c, d}) = 1 := by
  sorry

/--
Every measurable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with infinite measure contains the vertices of an
isosceles triangle of area $1$.

Koizumi [Ko25] has resolved this question, proving that any set with infinite measure must
contain the vertices of an isosceles trapezoid, an isosceles triangle, and a right-angled
triangle, all of area $1$.

Note the area condition forces `a`, `b`, `c` to be affinely independent, so no separate
non-degeneracy hypothesis is needed.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 28 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/110d489ed5c07e5b216453e092e9113127c98c9a/problems/353/Erdos353.lean"]
theorem erdos_353.variants.isosceles_triangle :
    ∀ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A → volume A = ⊤ →
      ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, ∃ c ∈ A,
        IsIsosceles a b c ∧
        volume (convexHull ℝ {a, b, c}) = 1 := by
  sorry

/--
Every measurable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with infinite measure contains the vertices of a
right-angled triangle of area $1$.

Koizumi [Ko25] has resolved this question, proving that any set with infinite measure must
contain the vertices of an isosceles trapezoid, an isosceles triangle, and a right-angled
triangle, all of area $1$.

Note the area condition forces `a`, `b`, `c` to be affinely independent, so no separate
non-degeneracy hypothesis is needed.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 28 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/110d489ed5c07e5b216453e092e9113127c98c9a/problems/353/Erdos353.lean"]
theorem erdos_353.variants.right_angled_triangle :
    ∀ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A → volume A = ⊤ →
      ∃ a ∈ A, ∃ b ∈ A, ∃ c ∈ A,
        IsRightAngled a b c ∧
        volume (convexHull ℝ {a, b, c}) = 1 := by
  sorry

/--
Every measurable $A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with infinite measure contains the vertices of a
cyclic quadrilateral of area $1$.

Kovač and Predojević [KoPr24] have proved that this is true for cyclic quadrilaterals - that
is, every set with infinite measure contains four distinct points on a circle such that the
quadrilateral determined by these four points has area $1$. The quadrilateral determined by
four distinct concyclic points is their convex hull.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 28 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/110d489ed5c07e5b216453e092e9113127c98c9a/problems/353/Erdos353.lean"]
theorem erdos_353.variants.cyclic_quadrilateral :
    ∀ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A → volume A = ⊤ →
      ∃ Q : Set ℝ², Q ⊆ A ∧ Q.ncard = 4 ∧ Cospherical Q ∧
        volume (convexHull ℝ Q) = 1 := by
  sorry

/--
The answer is negative for convex polygons with congruent sides: Kovač and Predojević
[KoPr24] prove that there exists a set of infinite measure such that every convex polygon
with congruent sides and all vertices in the set has area $<1$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 28 51, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/Jayyhk/erdos-lean/blob/110d489ed5c07e5b216453e092e9113127c98c9a/problems/353/Erdos353.lean"]
theorem erdos_353.variants.congruent_sides :
    ∃ A : Set ℝ², MeasurableSet A ∧ volume A = ⊤ ∧
      ∀ (n : ℕ) (v : Fin (n + 3) → ℝ²),
        IsCcwConvexPolygon v → (∀ i, v i ∈ A) →
        (∀ i, dist (v i) (v (i + 1)) = dist (v 0) (v 1)) →
        volume (convexHull ℝ (Set.range v)) < 1 := by
  sorry

end Erdos353

reformulations.difference: The trapezoid predicate uses strict convex position, parallel opposite supporting lines, and equal diagonals, rather than an explicit symmetry or equal-base-angle condition.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: This is the classical characterization of an isosceles trapezoid. In coordinates a=(0,0), b=(B,0), c=(x+C,h), d=(x,h), with B,C>0 and h≠0, equal diagonals give (x+C)^2=(x−B)^2, hence x=(B−C)/2. Thus the bases have a common perpendicular bisector and the trapezoid is symmetric. Conversely that symmetry gives equal diagonals. Its vertices can be ordered in the orientation required by the predicate without changing the convex hull or area.

reformulations.difference: The quadrilateral is represented by an unordered set Q with Q.ncard = 4 and Cospherical Q, without a separate ordered-polygon or convexity condition.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Q.ncard = 4 forces Q to be finite with four distinct elements; infinite sets have ncard zero. Cosphericity then supplies a positive-radius circle in the Euclidean plane. Four distinct points on a circle are all extreme points of their convex hull, and their circular ordering forms a nondegenerate convex cyclic quadrilateral. Its area is exactly the volume of that hull. Conversely, the vertex set of such a quadrilateral satisfies these conditions.

reformulations.difference: The universal area bound is stated only for the orientation selected by IsCcwConvexPolygon, whereas the source does not specify an orientation.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Reversing a cyclic enumeration by i ↦ −i on Fin (n+3) changes its orientation while preserving its vertex set, convex hull, and equal-side condition. Therefore a bound for the selected orientation is equivalent to the same bound for both orientations. This equivalence was proved in /workspace/review/scratch.lean as Review353.congruent_sides_orientation_iff, independently of the admitted problem theorems.

review.notes: All five declarations match the posed problem or the explicitly cited stronger negative result. Scratch Lean checks compiled successfully: unit area forces triangle affine independence, trapezoid vertices are distinct, four cospherical points have positive radius, and Fin addition includes the closing edge. The Borel-versus-completed-Lebesgue distinction is harmless here: measurable almost-everywhere-equal subsets preserve infinite measure, and the configuration assertions are hereditary in the appropriate direction; corresponding equivalences were also proved in scratch. Concrete geometry tests accept a square and reject a nonrectangular parallelogram as an isosceles trapezoid. The external proof's conclusions match the file, and its source contains no sorry or custom axioms. Recompilation under the sandbox's newer Lean 4.33.1 produced compatibility errors; its pinned Lean 4.28.0 build was not independently reverified. This does not contradict the recorded status.
